> 師。貞，丈人吉，無咎。

師 means teacher in modern Chinese. In the 易 it means an army — and the route from one to the other runs through a very specific original sense.

## 師 is 2,500 men

說文: 師，二千五百人為師 — the original sense is a unit of military organization.

From the unit comes 眾, the many (the 彖 opens with 師，眾也). From 眾 comes 師長, the one who leads and teaches; 師氏 was the office in charge of instruction.

The order matters, and the transmitted draft has it backwards: not "many" extended to "an army," but unit → many → teacher.

First the formation, then the people in it. That order is useful for the hexagram, because 師 is never about having many people. It is about a body of people that has a formation.

地中有水 — water hidden under the earth, as people are held within a territory. Gather them and it becomes 師. The army is not imported; it grows out of 民.

## 丈人 is not an old man

丈人: the mature and weighty, 嚴莊之稱, a term of gravity rather than age (Wang Bi).

丈 takes its force not from years but from the fact that no one treats him lightly.

Which is the actual job description in the text: 能持正、知進退 — able to hold the standard, and to know when to advance and when to stop.

## 律 is a pitch, not just a rule

師出以律.

律 is pitch, measure, law — all three at once in the archaic word.

And choosing that character is the hexagram's craft: a body of men on the move has to step on one beat. Law and time signature in a single word.

否臧凶: whether the discipline is good or bad, the absence of it is fatal. The line does not distinguish between good discipline and bad discipline at the outset — it distinguishes between having a measure and having none.

## 次 is a camp of more than two nights

左次無咎.

左傳 defines the vocabulary precisely: 一宿為舍，再宿為信，過信為次 — one night is a stop, two nights is a halt, more than two is 次.

So 左次 is not "he paused." It is: he chose ground and encamped, with measure.

Retreating and encamping properly is listed as 無咎 — the hexagram treats a well-made withdrawal as correct conduct, not as a lesser outcome.

## 輿尸 has two readings, and they are one thing

六三 師或輿尸.

First reading: 輿 is a cart, 尸 a corpse — a cart carrying the dead home, the image of defeat.

Second reading, Wang Bi's: 輿，眾也。尸，主也 — many masters. Everyone holding his own authority, no one unified.

The two are the two ends of one event: many masters is the cause, the cart of bodies is the result.

This book keeps both: the mechanism is 眾主無統, the image is 載尸而歸.

And the reason it happens here is structural: a yin line in a yang position, neither central nor correct, attempting the work that belongs to line two. Multiple heads in an army begin exactly like that.

## 田有禽，利執言

There are beasts in the field; it is beneficial to take them and speak of it.

The justification for using force is given as a fact about the field, not about the will: something is damaging the crop. Not "we are strong" — "the field has animals in it."

## 開國承家，小人勿用

After the campaign, fiefs are granted and houses established — and the hexagram's last instruction is a prohibition: do not employ the small man here.

Which is the hexagram's own knowledge that the danger after a war is not the enemy. It is the distribution.

## A test

Take a group you are responsible for. Ask whether it has 律 — one beat everyone is stepping on — or merely 眾, a count of people. The count is what 師 is not.
